Structural linguistics is an approach to the study of language that treats it as a system of interrelated elements—sounds, words, and structures—whose meaning derives from their relations to one another rather than from inherent properties. Dominant from the early twentieth century through the nineteen-fifties, it laid the groundwork for modern linguistic science before being reshaped by generative approaches. Pioneered by Ferdinand de Saussure, who distinguished between langue, the system of language, and parole, actual speech. Structural linguistics analyzes language as a closed system, a network of binary oppositions and relations where meaning emerges from differences—for instance, the sounds p and b create distinct meanings. Leonard Bloomfield developed American structural linguistics, emphasizing observable, distributional methods and rejecting introspection. The approach extends beyond words to entire systems: phonological, grammatical, and semantic structures all exhibit hierarchical organization. Structural methods influenced broader structuralist movements in anthropology through Claude Lévi-Strauss, in psychoanalysis, and in literary criticism. Noam Chomsky critiqued structural approaches as inadequate to explain language's recursive depth and productivity, and his work transformed linguistics by rejecting strict behaviorism and structural methods in favor of generative principles. The broader discipline of linguistics encompasses structuralism as a historical and methodological school.
